article.title: Choose a Personal Injury Lawyer
article.author: Sejal Desai
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. After a slip in a Florida hotel lobby, a Maryland visitor might receive treatment locally and fly home still wearing a brace. Choosing a lawyer then means deciding whether to hire someone near home or near the accident. Compare each candidate's authority to handle the case, experience with your kind of accident, communication plan, and written fee terms. Office location alone won't answer those questions. Start with a lawyer who can handle the case in the right place Three questions can get tangled together after an interstate accident: where you live, where the injury happened, and where a lawyer may practice. Which court can hear a claim, which state's law applies, and whether a particular lawyer can appear each require separate analysis. The accident state does not automatically control all of them, and it is not always the only possible place to file. Florida offers a concrete illustration. Florida Statutes section 48.193 lists committing a tortious act within the state as a basis for jurisdiction, or a court's authority to hear claims arising from that act. The incident location matters, but a lawyer must still assess the other requirements. Florida's limited-appearance process addresses a separate issue: an out-of-state lawyer seeking permission to appear in a Florida court files a motion. The court decides whether to grant it; the Bar's administrative processing does not grant permission. Verify the individual lawyer. Look up the lawyer in the official bar directory for the state where the case may be filed, and confirm current eligibility to practice. Check discipline records too. The Florida Bar posts public attorney discipline documents for the past 10 years and explains how to request older records. A blank recent history does not establish whether older discipline exists. Ask who will handle the local legal work. A lawyer near your home in Maryland may be able to help with a Florida claim by working with local counsel, a lawyer authorized to practice there. Have each candidate explain who would handle filings and court appearances, whether court permission would be needed, and who takes responsibility for the case as a whole. Have deadlines checked promptly. Filing periods vary by state and claim type. Don't assume returning home, negotiating with an insurer, or arranging a consultation extends a deadline. Ask the lawyer to review the incident date, the type of claim, the parties involved, and any notice requirements. Compare how each lawyer would handle your case Once you've checked a candidate's authorization, ask how the lawyer would manage your matter after you return home. Relevant experience. The Florida Bar's hiring guidance recommends asking how much experience the attorney has in cases like yours. A rental-car collision, a fall beside a hotel pool, and a boating injury raise different evidence questions. Ask about the same accident category and comparable evidence problems. Have the lawyer explain their familiarity with the procedures in the court where a lawsuit might be filed. For an accident in Boca Raton, Werner Hoffman Greig & Garcia describes car-accident representation and slip-and-fall services that include negotiating with the opposing party. Those service descriptions give you specific areas to discuss when asking about similar cases and who would handle yours. Werner Hoffman Greig & Garcia also offers a free case consultation, an opportunity to ask about the proposed representation and its terms. Confirm any fees for ongoing work and whether the firm has agreed to accept your case. A clear point of contact. The Bar's hiring guidance also recommends asking about both the means and frequency of case communication. Ask who will do the day-to-day work, who answers your questions, whether updates arrive by phone, email, or a client portal, and how often. A plan for participating from home. Ask how medical records from both states will be collected and whether video meetings are available. Have the lawyer explain which events, such as a deposition, a medical examination, or a hearing, could require you to travel. Ask what can happen remotely and what remains uncertain. Bring the documents you already have: the incident date and location, police or incident reports, photographs, witness contact details, medical records from both states, insurance correspondence, and records of lost income. Don't delay asking about deadlines while you gather them. During the consultation, ask what evidence is still needed and what uncertainties may affect the claim. Understand the written fee agreement before deciding Attorney fees versus case expenses. Under a contingency arrangement, the attorney's fee depends on a recovery. The Florida Bar's consumer guidance notes that you may also be responsible for costs and expenses if the agreement requires it. On its Boca Raton car-accident page, Werner Hoffman Greig & Garcia describes payment as contingent on winning or settling. Ask for the specific fee calculation and expense terms in your proposed agreement. Have every candidate explain the percentage or calculation method, which expenses are deducted, whether costs come out before or after the fee is calculated, and who pays expenses if the case does not succeed. Apply the same math to any early offer from an insurer , since accepting a settlement usually means signing a release that ends further claims from the accident. A free consultation does not answer these questions about representation costs. Scope and responsibility. Check whether the agreement addresses additional lawyers, local counsel, litigation if a lawsuit is filed, and any appeal. Ask which services are included and which would require a separate arrangement. Review the written agreement rather than relying on a firm's website to understand your obligations. Review your cancellation rights. In Florida, the Bar's client-rights guide says a contingent-fee contract must be in writing and gives the client three business days to reconsider it. This is a Florida-specific provision. Ask how to give written notice and whether any actual costs remain payable if you cancel. If you need help finding a candidate, a bar referral service is one option. The Florida Bar's service advertises a 30-minute consultation for no more than $25. That charge covers the consultation, not ongoing representation; other referral programs may have different arrangements. This article provides general information, not legal advice. Ask appropriately authorized counsel to review the deadlines and options for your situation.
